profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between two co-authors preparing an updated systematic literature review on business intelligence and big data in hospitality and tourism, extending a prior review that covered publications up to 2016. The meeting takes place at the start of the project after a funding office encouraged them to produce a publishable update within three months. Their agenda is to agree on the review scope, divide the screening and coding work, decide what counts as the core article set, and set milestones for a protocol draft, initial search, coding, and synthesis. The expected outcome is a shared plan for how the review will be executed, who will handle each part, and when the first complete evidence table and narrative synthesis will be ready.

members.name: Dr. Elena Marquez
members.role: Hospitality Management Associate Professor and lead author
members.expertise: Tourism analytics, hospitality research methods, review papers, theory building in service management
members.background: Elena has published review and conceptual papers in hospitality journals and previously used database-driven article screening with graduate assistants. She is comfortable framing interdisciplinary work for management audiences and is leading the academic positioning of this update.
members.private_state: She wants the update to read as a direct continuation of the earlier review so it is easier to publish in a hospitality journal, and she is worried that adding too much technical material or too many adjacent fields will make the review feel diffuse and harder to code consistently.
hidden_assumptions: An 'updated review' should preserve the same intellectual boundary as the earlier hospitality-and-tourism review, mainly adding newer publications rather than redefining the field.
The 'core set' of articles means papers published in hospitality and tourism journals, with computer science or information systems papers used only as contextual background if needed.

When they say they will 'replicate the prior method,' this includes keeping the same broad coding logic and article-level manual coding rather than redesigning the protocol around newer evidence-synthesis practices.

A paper is 'coded' once the article-level variables are entered into the shared evidence table by one trained reviewer and lightly checked during synthesis rather than independently double-coded from the start.

members.name: Dr. Victor Chen
members.expertise: Business intelligence, big data pipelines, bibliometrics, evidence synthesis workflows, interdisciplinary digital research
members.background: Victor works on analytics adoption across service industries and often collaborates with domain scholars on review studies. He has experience with reproducible review protocols, bibliometric mapping, and semi-automated abstract screening tools.
members.private_state: He wants the paper to look methodologically current and visibly interdisciplinary, and he hopes to use the project to demonstrate a stronger integration of management and data science than prior tourism reviews typically show.
hidden_assumptions: An 'updated review' should revisit the field as it now exists, including adjacent information systems and analytics outlets that materially shape hospitality and tourism practice.

The 'core set' means all studies materially about hospitality or tourism BI/big data, regardless of whether they appear in hospitality journals, information systems journals, or conference proceedings commonly indexed in Scopus.

When they say they will 'replicate the prior method,' this means preserving the main search concepts while upgrading execution with reproducible screening logs, software-assisted de-duplication, and more formal reliability checks.
A paper is only truly 'coded' after two reviewers have applied the coding frame or at least calibrated on a substantial subset with explicit agreement thresholds.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the updated review scope
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to do an 'update of the 2016 review' and to 'keep it comparable.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means extending the prior review forward in time while keeping roughly the same disciplinary boundary centered on hospitality and tourism management journals.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means updating the topic to the contemporary field while still comparing with the older review, including relevant information systems and analytics outlets that study hospitality/tourism contexts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see continuity with the earlier paper as obviously desirable, and 'comparable' sounds precise enough that neither thinks to unpack whether comparability applies to time period only or also to disciplinary boundaries.

misalignment_points.topic: Meaning of the core article set
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree first to build the 'core set' before adding supporting material.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 uses 'core set' to mean the final review sample of hospitality and tourism journal articles that will populate the main tables and counts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 uses 'core set' to mean the master included evidence base across all indexed publication venues relevant to the topic, from which subsets can later be filtered by venue.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is common in review planning and usually sounds like a harmless sequencing choice; each assumes the other shares the same default review vocabulary.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to replicate the prior method
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'replicate the prior method as closely as possible.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes they will mirror the prior study's manually curated search-and-code workflow, using database exports, spreadsheet screening, and article-level coding categories aligned with the original paper.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes they will preserve the original conceptual categories but modernize the workflow through review software, explicit PRISMA-style logging, automated de-duplication, and calibration rounds before full coding.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are trying to honor the earlier study rather than argue for a different design, so the phrase 'as closely as possible' masks different assumptions about whether process modernization changes the method or merely implements it better.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the evidence table should be 'fully coded' before synthesis starts.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks 'fully coded' means every included article has all agreed fields completed once in the spreadsheet so they can begin writing patterns and gaps.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'fully coded' means the coding frame has been applied with documented consistency, including at least a reliability check or dual coding for a substantial portion before synthesis can legitimately proceed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both treat coding completeness as a routine milestone, and because neither wants to bog down the planning meeting in methodological minutiae, they use the same milestone language while silently applying different standards.

turns.inner_thought: I need to anchor this as a direct continuation of the 2016 hospitality-and-tourism review, not a reinvention. If we keep the same boundary and just extend the timeline, the paper will be easier to position for a hospitality journal and the coding will stay manageable within three months.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Victor. Given the funding office timeline, I think the cleanest way to frame this is as an update of the 2016 review. We should keep it comparable, but extend the field map into the present so the contribution is immediately visible.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, comparable to the old review in the broad concepts and historical benchmark, but the field now spills across information systems and analytics venues too. If we don't reflect that evolution, the update will look dated before it's even submitted.
turns.utterance: I agree. Starting from the earlier search concepts makes sense, and if we keep it comparable we can still show how the BI and big data landscape around hospitality has evolved over time. That should make the update feel both grounded and current.

turns.inner_thought: First priority is to lock down the actual review sample from the hospitality and tourism journals we can defend in the main tables. If we stabilize that early from Scopus and Web of Science, I can keep the project from ballooning into adjacent literatures.
turns.utterance: For milestones, I'd suggest we first build the core set from Scopus and Web of Science. If we can stabilize that early, everything downstream becomes much easier.

turns.inner_thought: Good—I'll create a master included evidence base from both databases, then we can break it out later by venue type, journal family, or topic cluster. That gives us flexibility without losing comparability.
turns.utterance: That works for me. I'll assemble the core set first, and once that pool is in place we can slice it by journal family and topic clusters as needed.

turns.inner_thought: I want the coding categories to line up closely with the original review's article-level fields—research topic, methods, data source, analytical focus—so we can compare periods cleanly and avoid methodological overcomplication.
turns.utterance: Exactly. And on the method side, I'd really like us to replicate the prior method as closely as possible so the article features, research topics, and data categories line up with the original review.

turns.inner_thought: Preserve the original concepts, yes—but implement them with a current review workflow so the process is reproducible and publication-ready. I can set up proper screening logs and a cleaner review pipeline without changing the substantive design.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I can set up the review workflow so that we replicate the prior method as closely as possible while keeping the whole process clean, reproducible, and straightforward to document once the database records come in.

turns.inner_thought: Good—he can handle the front-end database work, and I'll shape the coding sheet around the old review's logic and draft the framing. Once he organizes the records, I can move quickly into article-level coding for the hospitality sample.
turns.utterance: Then maybe we split it this way: I'll refine the coding sheet and start shaping the introduction and positioning, and you handle the search export, de-duplication, and initial record organization. That should get the core set moving without too much delay.

turns.inner_thought: Before full extraction, we really should calibrate the coding frame on a subset so we have some evidence of consistency. If we do that early, the evidence table will be defensible once it's fully coded.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. Once the records are organized, I'd also suggest a short calibration pass so we're aligned before the evidence table is fully coded.

turns.inner_thought: A brief check-in on the coding sheet is fine, but I don't want this turning into a long reliability exercise. As soon as each article has its fields entered, I can start identifying patterns and writing the synthesis sections.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's sensible. Once the evidence table is fully coded, I can begin drafting the synthesis around fragmentation in the literature, methods trends, and the main emerging gaps.

turns.inner_thought: If we move efficiently, I can get the search and screening done in two weeks, then we can spend the next month on coding with the calibration built in. After that, visual mapping from the coded set should be quick and add a modern touch.
turns.utterance: In terms of timing, I think we can do the search and screening in the first two weeks, use the following month to get the coding closed, and then build the visual mapping from the coded set right after that.

turns.inner_thought: This sounds workable as long as we keep the review bounded and don't let the sample sprawl. If the core set is locked early and the method stays close to the prior paper, I can push the narrative synthesis fast enough for submission.
turns.utterance: Great. So we're aligned on keeping the update comparable, finalizing the core set early, and replicating the prior method as closely as possible while moving quickly toward synthesis. That should give us a solid draft path.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll send over the search strings, workflow setup, and milestone dates today so we can start screening next week and keep the whole process transparent from the beginning.
